Female Kuhl's pipistrelles give birth to altricial neonates with an average birth mass of just 1.35 grams [Wwb = 1.35 grams], an adaptation typical of vespertilionid bats that allows for a relatively short gestation period while shifting the energetic burden of growth to lactation. This low neonatal mass, representing less than a quarter of the mother's body weight, facilitates the production of litters despite the female's own small size. The pups are born with their eyes closed and rely entirely on milk for nourishment during the initial period following parturition.

In contrast, the ultimate wet weight of an adult female reaches approximately 6 grams [Wwi = approximately 6 grams], representing a remarkable fourfold and a half increase from the birth weight. This substantial mass gain is accomplished through a combination of efficient milk conversion during the suckling stage and subsequent high-protein insectivory after weaning. Adult females must attain this body mass to successfully sustain the energetic demands of gestation and lactation, particularly in the temperate and Mediterranean climates where this species is common.

When examined at a stable body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], the gestation period for Kuhl's pipistrelle lasts about 42 days [tg = about 42 days]. This value is derived from studies on the closely related Pipistrellus pipistrellus and is considered representative for P. kuhlii under similar thermal conditions. The duration aligns well with the typical gestation lengths observed among other small-bodied, temperate-zone vespertilionids, where metabolic rate and maternal body temperature dictate developmental speed.

The time elapsed since birth at which weaning occurs has been documented at approximately 42 days [tx = approximately 42 days], again measured at a body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] based on comparative data from Pipistrellus pipistrellus. This period of lactation dependency is crucial for the juvenile to achieve sufficient body size and flight capability. After nutritional independence is attained, the young must continue to forage intensively to build the fat reserves necessary for surviving their first winter hibernation.

Puberty in female Kuhl's pipistrelles is reached at a time since birth of around 256 days [tp = around 256 days], as extrapolated from growth studies on Pipistrellus pipistrellus under a consistent body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This timing means that young born early in the summer typically reach sexual maturity late the following spring. The maximum reproductive rate for this species involves approximately 1.5 pups per year [Ri = approximately 1.5 pups per year] under controlled conditions. A plausible maximum lifespan under these thermal conditions is in the range of 8 years [am = 8 years], though wild individuals likely face substantially higher mortality from predation and resource limitation at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C].
